title: Electret field plates in isolation trenches defuse GIDL hot spots
idea: Effect: electret fixed charge. A permanently charged dielectric (Al2O3 with ~1e13 q/cm^2 of fixed negative charge, or implant-charged SiO2) lines the isolation trench beside each storage junction, counter-biasing the junction edge where band-to-band tunneling GIDL peaks; this cuts the peak field ~30% and tail leakage ~10x with no wiring.
why: 10x density: shrinking pitch 3x raises junction fields and blows up tails; passive electret field shaping keeps 64 ms retention for 0.5 fF caps in densely stacked lateral cells (~10x) at the cost of one liner deposition.

title: Eliminate the fixed sense reference: pilot cells set each row's threshold
idea: Each row carries a few pilot cells written to known 0/1 values at every write. On read, the sense amp's reference comes from the pilots' current levels, the way wireless receivers use pilot symbols, so it tracks decay, temperature and drift of the <=400 C devices.
why: Removes drift and leakage guard-bands for low-thermal-budget transistors, extending effective retention ~2-4x and lowering read errors with no extra reads.

title: Nonvolatile fault-map sidecar remembers weak cells across power cycles
idea: Rearrange where reliability knowledge lives: a small MRAM chiplet patterned by argon ion-beam etching (no fluorinated chemistry) is co-packaged with each DRAM stack and stores per-row retention classes, hammer thresholds and patch lists, so profiling survives power-off and travels with the module.
why: Makes field profiling, per-row refresh and host-owned repair practical without re-profiling at every boot.

title: Adaptive twin-cell pairing retires weak cells into differential bits
idea: When test or field ECC finds a weak cell, a fuse pairs it with its neighbor as a 2T2C differential bit sensed on complementary bitlines. Differential sensing doubles the signal and cancels common-mode leakage, so the tail cell stops limiting refresh. The cost is about 0.1% of capacity.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): refresh is set by the 0.1% tail rather than the 1e-9 tail, for ~2-4x longer intervals.

title: Eliminate spare rows and fuses: base-die CAM remaps failing blocks
idea: Remove redundant rows and columns and the laser/e-fuse blocks from the DRAM core. An HBM/CXL logic die holds a CAM plus a spare SRAM/DRAM pool that remaps any failing 64 B block at any point in life. The CAM is filled from test results and field ECC events.
why: Redundancy plus fuses take ~3-6% of the die, and repair is one-shot; lifelong, fine-grained remap recovers that area and saves dies with clustered defects.

title: Selective-assembly die pairing matches complementary defect maps
idea: Bearing makers measure parts and mate oversized balls with undersized races; record each die's failing and weak-row map at wafer test and pair dies into stacks or ranks whose bad addresses do not overlap, so cheap module-level mirroring or spare sharing covers one die's holes with its partner's good rows.
why: Rescues dies that exceed on-die redundancy (several yield points) and makes cross-die repair nearly free because overlaps are engineered to near zero.

title: Power-electronics snubber: slew-shaped wordline edges cut hammer disturbance
idea: Adapted from snubbers and slew-rate control that suppress ringing and EMI in power converters: wordline drivers use a programmable current-starved two-segment edge (fast to ~70%, then slow ramp, and a slow falling tail), reducing dV/dt coupling and the abrupt trap-assisted electron emission at wordline fall that drives row hammer and RowPress flips.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): disturbance scales with edge rate and injection at wordline fall; shaped edges may raise flip thresholds 2-4x at a ~1-2 ns tRAS/tRP cost, shrinking mitigation-refresh overhead.

title: Cray's SRAM main memory revived at near-threshold with ECC-mapped Vmin failures
idea: Cray-1 and other supercomputers used SRAM main memory until DRAM's cost won. Fix the cost and power that killed it: CFET-stacked 6T SRAM in monolithic 3D tiers run at ~0.45 V, where leakage collapses but ~1e-4 cells fail, with a test-time row-sparing map plus SECDED absorbing the low-Vmin failures.
why: Static storage: zero refresh, no capacitor, buildable in U.S. logic fabs; ECC turns low-voltage unreliability into a ~4x leakage cut.

title: Tick-to-trade speculation: use data before strong ECC finishes
idea: High-frequency trading systems act on market data before full validation and unwind on the rare error. Inside the host memory controller, forward the raw 64 B line at normal latency while a heavier decoder (two-symbol-correcting Reed-Solomon over a burst pair) runs in the background. If it disagrees, the core replays dependent instructions through its existing branch-mispredict machinery. Standard DDR5/HBM bursts carry exactly the same bits.
why: Strong ECC normally adds 5-10 ns of latency, so vendors lean on stronger cells instead. Hiding decode latency enables chipkill-class correction on every access and tolerates ~10x weaker raw cell populations at no latency cost (facts 1, 3).

title: Glial potassium buffering: buried sink lines soak up hammer electrons
idea: Astrocytes mop up excess K+ so neighbouring neurons do not fire spuriously; add a buried, positively biased n+ 'glial' collector line in the isolation between adjacent access transistors that captures electrons emitted by the aggressor wordline's trap-assisted charge pumping before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: a physical root-cause fix; raising the threshold even 10x removes most tracker and victim-refresh overhead.

title: Substitute passing-gate coupling with a buried negative-biased shield plate
idea: Insert a thin conductive shield line, held at a negative bias, between each buried wordline and the neighboring storage-node junction, so hammering electrons and coupling from the aggressor gate end on the shield instead of the victim node.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): aims to push flip threshold from ~1k back to >50k activations, removing most mitigation refresh and periphery logic.

title: Chameleon cells: auto-switch 1T1C to twin-cell 2T2C above 105 C
idea: Wordline decoders support a paired mode where two adjacent rows store complementary data on one sense amp (differential twin cell); above 105 C the OS shrinks the hot region and the controller migrates its pages into paired mode, doubling signal margin.
why: Twin cells tolerate ~4-10x more leakage, so parts survive 125 C for 10 years while cooler deployments keep full 1T1C density - no cell designed for worst case.

title: Evaporating pheromone memory: never refresh data born to expire
idea: Ant pheromone trails are useful because they evaporate; an allocator API lets software tag buffers (activations, KV-cache spills, packets, shuffle data) with a time-to-live shorter than the region's measured retention, and the controller never refreshes those rows, simply reclaiming them at expiry.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth: transient buffers are a large share of AI traffic and live microseconds to milliseconds; zero refresh for them saves their share of 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth.

title: Canary quorum: deliberately weak sentinel rows set the refresh rate
idea: Like canaries in a mine combined with bacterial quorum sensing, each bank carries a few rows built with ~30% smaller capacitance; the controller lengthens the refresh interval until a quorum of canaries across the die begins to flip and then backs off, so the main array always runs at the largest safe interval for its real temperature and age.
why: Refresh is set by worst-case datasheet margin (64 ms at 85 C); live canary feedback could run typical parts at 4-8x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: Quarter refresh energy: bit-plane layout refreshes only MSB rows
idea: Imposed limit: refresh energy cut by 75%. The controller transposes int8/fp8 tensors into bit-planes stored in separate rows. MSB-plane rows refresh at the normal rate, and LSB-plane rows refresh 8-16x less often and are allowed to decay.
why: Fact 3: ~60-70% of refresh energy is cut with less than 0.1% model-quality loss for inference weights and activations.

title: Substitute per-write ferroelectric switching with power-event-only polarization snapshot
idea: A DRAM capacitor gets a thin ferroelectric HZO liner that stays unpolarized-active in normal DRAM mode (charge only); a power-fail detector fires one global 'snapshot' pulse that writes each cell's charge state into polarization, and recall happens at power-up.
why: NV without the FE fatigue problem: the ferroelectric is cycled only per power event (~1e4 in life), so DRAM-mode endurance stays unlimited while refresh-on-idle can be fully powered off.

title: Sourdough starter: OS-donated cold pages become living spare rows
idea: Like a starter fed from each batch, an OS balloon driver donates 0.5-1% of free pages to the memory controller, which remaps rows showing correctable-error growth or hammer susceptibility into them; pages are handed back under memory pressure and the starter is re-fed from the next free batch.
why: Lets fabs ship dies with 5-10x more weak rows than the fused-spare budget allows; raises sellable bits per wafer ~3-8% and extends field life with zero capex.

title: ArchShield fault maps replaced by in-row stuck-aware scrambler masks
idea: ArchShield-style weak-cell fault maps died on lookup latency and OS-reserved memory. Fix: leaky cells only lose the charged state, so treat them as 'partially stuck at 0' (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov defect coding); each row stores its weak-cell positions in a few spare cells that are read for free when the row opens, and on-die logic picks one of 4-8 scrambler masks that leaves those cells discharged, saving the mask ID with the line.
why: Retention-weak cells stop causing errors at ~0.5% overhead, so smaller-Cs or leakier cells become acceptable (charge wall fact 1, leakage tail fact 3).

title: Substitute device non-volatility with replication across independent power domains
idea: Keep cheap volatile DRAM but replicate each write synchronously to a second memory node on a separate power feed and UPS (RDMA/CXL mirroring), so a single power loss never loses data.
why: Delivers persistence with today's DRAM supply and no new device risk; costs 2x capacity only for data that must persist (~10-20% of footprint).

title: Eliminate the end-of-life cliff: ECC rate that grows with age
idea: Partition memory into regions whose code rate the controller can reprogram, e.g. from 64/72 up to 64/80. When scrubbing reports rising error rates from aging, VRT or hammer damage, a region trades capacity for a stronger code and the OS shrinks its advertised size.
why: Allows shipping lower-margin dies and extends fleet module life 2-3x, cutting replacement demand during the shortage.

title: Double-stitched hot rows halve activations per physical copy
idea: Tailors double-stitch seams at stress points; for read-hot rows the controller keeps a duplicate in a distant subarray and alternates or randomises activations between copies (writes go to both), so each physical row sees 1/k of the activation rate.
why: Raises the effective hammer threshold k-fold for read-mostly hot data such as weights and page tables without counters or neighbour refresh (fact 9); the twin also backs up a retention-failed copy.

title: Electrochromic contact images capacitor-dielectric defects across whole wafer
idea: Effect: electrochromism. After the capacitor dielectric step and before the top plate, a removable transparent electrolyte-plus-WO3 electrochromic contact is pressed onto the wafer and the bottom electrodes are biased through the substrate; cells whose dielectric leaks (pinholes, thin spots, pA-nA) color the film locally, and an optical scan maps millions of defect sites in seconds into a mat-level repair or rework map.
why: Capacitor leakage is a major retention-tail contributor (facts 1, 3): defects are caught at the step instead of after full flow and hours of multi-temperature retention test, raising yield and cutting test cost and scrap.

title: Decay-as-scaling: analog weight memory that neural nets self-correct
idea: Ideal: decay that does not change the answer. Closest: store neural-net weights as analog charge in large 180 nm capacitors; cells in a row decay by nearly the same exponential factor, a uniform scaling that a per-row reference cell measures and normalization layers cancel, so only cell-to-cell mismatch counts as error.
why: Facts 3 and 5: removes refresh for slowly changing weights and stores ~4-6 effective bits per cell on legacy tools.

title: On-die ReRAM keeps the chip's own weak-cell map
idea: Inverts 'the DRAM die knows nothing about itself': one BEOL mask adds a small ReRAM array in the periphery that stores the die's evolving weak-cell and hammer map, so on-die logic applies erasure decoding and coset encoding at power-up with no external flash or retest.
why: Makes map-based tolerance self-contained and portable across systems; removes minutes of boot-time retention profiling.

title: Tardigrade tun state: idle pages dehydrate into strong code, slow refresh
idea: Tardigrades survive by shutting down into a protective tun; pages untouched for N seconds are compressed and rewritten with a heavy BCH/LDPC code in the space freed, and their rows move to a 10-30x slower refresh tier, rehydrating on first access.
why: Refresh at 32-64 Gb (16-33% of idle power): most memory is idle at any instant; strong coding absorbs the higher raw BER of seconds-long refresh, cutting idle refresh energy ~10x.

title: Decommissioned-server DRAM recertified by in-system retention retest
idea: Combine e-waste recycling with in-system profiling: retired DDR4/DDR5 modules pass through an automated rack that runs retention and hammer profiling, writes per-module weak-row maps into SPD and redeploys them behind stronger controller ECC as CXL-attached expansion.
why: Supply shortage: reclaims existing bits with no fab capital and US-located refurbishment, delivering usable memory at a fraction of new price.

title: Split wells so idle mats get local back-bias
idea: Inverts 'body bias is one global setting': one mask segments the array's deep well per mat, so in self-refresh the controller applies stronger negative back-bias only to mats holding mapped weak cells while active mats keep fast bias.
why: Cuts subthreshold leakage in weak mats ~10x during idle (fact 3) without slowing active access; ~2x self-refresh interval.

title: Expiring pages: data with a lifetime skips refresh entirely
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. The allocator tags pages with a time-to-live (activations, gradients, KV of a finished request); the controller keeps a per-row TTL table, stops refreshing rows whose data expires or will be overwritten before the retention limit, and steers short-TTL data into weak-retention rows that would otherwise set the bank's refresh rate.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3): AI training buffers often live <100 ms, so 40-70% of rows in those regions skip refresh; weak-tail rows become usable instead of forcing repair, a few % yield.

title: Aging-adaptive ECC: code strength rises as the module ages
idea: Rule: an aging module is re-formatted, never retired. Modules start life with light ECC to maximize capacity. As per-region error rates climb, firmware re-encodes regions into stronger codes (SEC-DED, then RS t=2, then t=4), trading capacity for reliability. Second-life buyers get a matured, highly reliable module at lower capacity.
why: Gives more bits early in life and extends usable life far beyond one fixed-code design.

title: Completion-detecting sense amps: weak cells read slow, not wrong
idea: Inverts 'memory timing is synchronous and fixed': each sense-amp group asserts a done signal once its latch resolves past a full-rail threshold; the bank uses this asynchronous handshake, so a low-charge weak cell simply takes 2-3 ns longer instead of being mis-sensed at a fixed tRCD.
why: Turns the charge/retention tail (facts 1, 3) from an error source into a small latency tail; strong cells finish ~15% faster than the worst-case timing.

title: K: potassium-40 half-life tags skip refresh for short-lived data
idea: Allocator APIs tag buffers with an expected lifetime, like a radioisotope half-life; the controller tracks per-row last-write time and suppresses refresh for rows whose data will be rewritten or freed before retention expires (activations, KV caches, DMA buffers).
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) in AI training memory, where most data lives under 64 ms.

title: Unused repair spares reborn as hammer-shadow and parity rows
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the 30-60% of redundant rows/columns left unused after repair get a second job; an on-die table exposes them so the controller migrates hammered hot rows into them and stores extra parity there for a stronger code.
why: Reclaims ~2-4% of die area already paid for as a live reliability resource; raises the effective hammer threshold and correction strength at zero extra silicon.

title: Back-gate calibration loop keeps Zn-Si-O gain cells centered
idea: Worse: drop indium and gallium from IGZO and accept drifting, unstable zinc-oxide transistors. Flip: build gain cells with an amorphous Zn-Si-O channel (Zn, Si, O only) and a per-mat back gate whose bias a calibration loop retunes every few seconds from reference cells, cancelling threshold drift from bias stress and temperature.
why: Fact 3 and scarce resources: keeps oxide-semiconductor ultra-low leakage (refresh intervals of seconds) without In or Ga, with drift handled by the system rather than by material perfection.

title: Drip irrigation: Esaki-diode trickle latch makes storage nodes self-sustaining
idea: Each storage node gets a vertical Si/SiGe interband tunnel diode to a bias line; its negative-differential-resistance curve against a matched load forms two stable voltages, so leakage is replenished continuously like drip irrigation rather than refreshed.
why: Eliminates refresh at 125 C if peak-to-valley ratio stays >~3 when hot (interband tunneling is weakly temperature dependent) and valley current stays <~10 fA/cell over 10 years.

title: Si: silicone microcapsule underfill self-heals cracks in memory stacks
idea: Formulate an underfill with PDMS healing-agent microcapsules and a tin catalyst (no platinum); a growing microcrack ruptures capsules and seals itself before moisture and stress concentrate on microbumps. A small formulation and dispensing line suffices.
why: Thermal-cycle cracking drives opens in HBM/3DS stacks (fact 6); target ~2x thermal-cycle life.

title: Eliminate permanent vacancy damage: oxygen-reservoir layer re-oxidizes channel defects
idea: Place an over-oxidized cap (IrOx or oxygen-rich HfO2 deposited at <=300 C) next to the oxide channel. A periodic low-voltage 'heal' bias drives oxygen ions back into the vacancy sites that formed under stress, electrochemically restoring off-current and threshold.
why: Makes aging-induced growth of the leakage tail reversible, holding retention for life and allowing cheaper, less stable low-temperature films.

title: Companion planting: pair hammer-heavy pages with self-healing neighbours
idea: Gardeners plant companions that protect each other. A kernel page allocator uses the reverse-engineered DRAM address map to put physically adjacent rows next to frequently activated pages. Those adjacent rows are filled with data that rewrites itself every few ms anyway (ring buffers, network and DMA rings, scratch), or with guard and free pages. Hammer victims therefore heal on their own.
why: Raises the effective hammer tolerance with no hardware change (fact 9), as a pure kernel patch within budget.

title: IceCube field updates: microcode-programmable on-die ECC decoder
idea: IceCube's sensors, frozen into Antarctic ice since 2010, receive firmware updates as new failure modes appear. Make on-die ECC a small programmable decoder, with code tables and a syndrome-to-action lookup in SRAM. Vendors can then push new codes, new bit interleaving and new hammer responses to deployed DRAM as a signed mode-register firmware load.
why: New error mechanisms (hammer at ~1k activations, new VRT modes) currently force respins or extra margin. Updatable decoding lets earlier, weaker silicon ship and stay safe (fact 9).

title: Elastic twin-cell mode switchable per row group
idea: Ideal: every bit is perfectly reliable but density is never wasted. Closest: a mode register lets the OS flip any row group between 1 cell per bit and 2-cell differential per bit (complementary data on the bitline pair), giving ~4x retention and hammer immunity; kernel, page tables and keys go to twin mode while bulk data stays dense.
why: Facts 3 and 9: hardens the ~2-5% of critical data at 2x cost instead of hardening all bits, so the rest of memory can run at relaxed refresh.

title: Park bitlines at the data's safe rail during standby
idea: Inverts 'bitlines idle at VDD/2': in self-refresh, columns whose mapped weak cells hold 1 are parked at VDD and others at ground, so residual subthreshold leakage through off access transistors flows toward the stored value instead of away from it.
why: Removes the subthreshold share of the retention tail for mapped weak cells; ~2x longer self-refresh interval, 10-15% idle power saved.

title: TI tunneling SRAM fixed with self-trimmed silicon interband tunnel diodes
idea: TI's tunneling SRAM (a resonant-tunneling diode pair latching a DRAM storage node) died because III-V peak currents varied too much across wafers. Fix: use low-temperature Si/SiGe interband tunnel diodes grown in BEOL, plus a per-mat replica diode and electrical trim pulse that sets the valley-current bias, so each node sits in one of two stable points with pA standby.
why: Static, zero-refresh cell near DRAM density, with the tunnel-diode latch restoring any leakage or hammer-induced charge loss (facts 3, 9).

title: Quarantine hot aggressor rows inside a moat subarray
idea: Flip mitigation from victims to aggressors: a row exceeding the hammer threshold is migrated into a small quarantine subarray where every occupied row is flanked by two never-used guard rows, so further hammering finds no victims; it migrates back when it cools.
why: Row hammer: replaces repeated victim refreshes (bandwidth tax) with one migration; costs ~0.5% capacity for the moat.

title: Read-port-isolated gain cell geometrically immune to read hammer
idea: Hammer needs aggressor toggles to couple into victim storage nodes. In a 3T gain cell, reads toggle only a read wordline on the read transistor's source, and the write wordline moves only on writes (~10x rarer). Shield write wordlines with grounded lines and size node coupling <0.5 mV per toggle, so a flip needs ~1e6 activations.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): threshold from ~1k to ~1M toggles, which removes TRR/counter logic area.

title: Foundry riser canary rows fail first and trigger group refresh
idea: Castings use risers so shrinkage defects form in sacrificial metal; give every 64-row group one 'riser' canary row of deliberately undersized capacitors with an added leak device, sitting in the same local thermal environment. A background scanner activates only canary rows and refreshes a group only when its canary has decayed past a guard threshold.
why: Refresh tracks real local leakage and temperature instead of the 64 ms worst-case tail (fact 3); scanning is 1/64 of activations, targeting ~3-6x fewer refresh operations for ~1.5% row overhead.

title: Shingled DRAM bands with built-in neighbour restore, like SMR drives
idea: Shingled magnetic recording overlaps tracks and accepts that a write must rewrite its neighbours. In the same way, rows are packed at a pitch that is deliberately weak to hammer and grouped into bands of 8-16. Each ACT also schedules a hidden pipelined restore of rows i+-1 in a parallel subarray slot, so the protection is built into the structure and does not depend on counters.
why: Designing for a hammer threshold of ~100 instead of ~1k (fact 9) frees about 10% of wordline pitch, giving a 10-15% density gain. The mitigation tables go away. The cost is extra restore energy on each ACT.

title: Multi-tenant cloud quarantine: tenants own whole subarrays plus guard rows
idea: Treat the hostile cloud tenant as the extreme user. Using the vendor's published row-to-subarray map, the hypervisor gives each VM whole subarrays (hammer disturbance does not cross the sense-amp stripe) and leaves a guard row at any shared boundary. Hammering then only disturbs the attacker's own data.
why: Removes cross-tenant hammer risk, so cells that flip at low activation counts can be used without expensive in-DRAM counters, at <1% guard overhead (fact 9).

title: Triple-row activation turns charge sharing into majority vote
idea: Ideal: redundancy computed for free by physics. Closest: in a 180 nm array each critical bit is written to three rows on the same bitlines; a read opens all three wordlines at once so charge sharing settles the bitline to the analog majority, masking any one decayed or flipped cell with no logic.
why: Fact 3: a 2-of-3 tolerant tier whose refresh can run ~10x slower; 3x area but zero ECC logic.

title: Twin-cell glass-panel DRAM with invalid-pair erasure decoding
idea: Box [medium: capacitor charge | access: LTPS planar TFT | sense: differential twin-cell | integration: chiplet | substrate: Gen-6 glass panel | fab: i-line/DUV panel litho]. Each bit is a complementary cell pair on cheap panel-made arrays; a pair that senses 00 or 11 (one cell leaked or dead) is flagged as an erasure, and a Reed-Solomon code over 32-pair symbols corrects ~2x more erasures than unknown errors.
why: Fact 4 capital: lets panel fabs with ~1e-3 raw cell failure ship usable working memory; ~2x cell area but ~10x lower capex per m2 of array.

title: Sixteen-subcell majority bits from nanoimprinted crossbars
idea: Box [medium: 16 nano-capacitors per bit | access: crossbar diode | sense: ensemble charge summing | integration: monolithic | substrate: glass | fab: nanoimprint lithography]. Each bit is a cluster of 16 sub-10 nm imprinted capacitors on one local bitline sensed as a summed charge, so up to ~5 dead or leaky subcells per bit change nothing.
why: Facts 1/4: swaps defect-free EUV patterning for defect-tolerant imprint; ~5x lower patterning cost per layer.

title: OFDM pilot cells that calibrate each row's sense reference
idea: OFDM inserts known pilot tones to estimate the channel. Each row stores a few pilot cells holding known 1s and 0s, rewritten at every restore. At sense time the pilots' developed bitline voltages set a row-specific sense reference. The reference therefore tracks how far that row has decayed since its last restore, and its temperature.
why: This recovers ~30% of sense margin, so Cs can drop toward ~3.5 fF (fact 1) or refresh can run 2x longer (fact 3).

title: Magnify supply by re-grading retired hyperscaler DIMMs behind host ECC
idea: Buy DIMMs from hyperscaler decommissioning, re-grade them with long in-system error telemetry and retention tests, and redeploy them as tier-2 memory behind CXL expanders that add chipkill-class host ECC.
why: Supply: adds roughly 10-20% usable memory with zero wafer starts and no new fab capital.

title: Relay computer revival: NEMS contact access switches with zero off-leakage
idea: Bell Labs and Harvard relay computers switched bits with metal contacts that had no leakage when open. Replace the access transistor with a vertical nano-electromechanical contact switch (a ~10 nm air-gap cantilever pulled in by the wordline) released with dry vapour HF, so an open cell has essentially no leakage path and retention is set by dielectric leakage (minutes) even at 125 C.
why: Water and refresh (facts 3, 10): removing the access-leakage tail lets memory run at 125 C with near-zero refresh, so datacentres can use dry coolers (>10x less water), and dry release avoids wet MEMS steps; contact wear (~1e15 cycles needed) is the main risk.

title: Plywood cross-grain tier rotation turns 3D line faults into single bits
idea: Plywood alternates grain 90 degrees so a split cannot run through the panel; in monolithic 3D DRAM, rotate each tier's wordline direction (or its logical bit-to-codeword map) relative to its neighbours and assemble codewords vertically across tiers, so one broken wordline in tier k becomes one bit in each of many codewords.
why: Tier-level line defects are the expected killer of 26+-tier 3D DRAM (fact 2); converting them into correctable single-bit errors could tolerate ~10x higher line-defect density per tier.

title: Unihemispheric sleep: half the array maintains while the other serves
idea: Dolphins and birds sleep one brain hemisphere at a time; split ultra-leaky, ultra-cheap arrays (retention ~1 ms) into twin hemispheres that alternate, one serving reads and writes while the other runs back-to-back refresh and scrubbing, with hot lines mirrored so service never stalls.
why: Admits capacitorless or tiny-capacitor cells with 50-100x worse retention (dropping the costliest high-AR capacitor module) by accepting ~50% maintenance duty and 2x mirroring of hot lines; a ~100x path when built on stacked cheap tiers.

title: One metal mask turns the same die into two reliability SKUs
idea: Inverts 'one die design has one reliability spec': a cheap upper-metal mask variant either routes the on-die ECC parity cells into the data path (approximate SKU, +12% capacity, no ECC) or keeps strong ECC with extended refresh (enterprise SKU).
why: The same wafers serve AI-tolerant and exact markets, raising sellable bits ~10% with no front-end process change.

title: Child's ice pack: printed phase-change wax pads keep DRAM below 85C
idea: A child puts an ice pack on a fever: thermal pads loaded with microencapsulated paraffin or salt-hydrate phase-change material are screen-printed or roll-to-roll coated onto DIMM heat spreaders and HBM lids; they absorb workload heat bursts as latent heat, so dies stay below the 85 C threshold that forces 2x refresh.
why: Fact 3: avoids double-refresh mode during bursts (refresh costs 10-20% of bandwidth at high density), and gentler thermal cycling slows solder and TSV fatigue.

title: Samsung's withdrawn PRAM fixed by checkerboard thermal-phase write scheduling
idea: Samsung's mobile PRAM never scaled partly because RESET heat partially crystallizes neighboring cells (thermal disturb). Fix: the write scheduler splits each array into four checkerboard phases and never writes adjacent cells within one thermal time constant (~100 ns), so each phase's idle neighbors act as heat sinks.
why: Permits ~30% tighter pitch (density) without disturb-induced retention loss.

title: Chilled-DIMM certification grade with 256 ms refresh
idea: Worse: run DRAM at 85-95 C, where leakage doubles every ~10 C. Flip: create a 'cold-loop' grade: modules on datacenter liquid cold plates held at 25-35 C are binned and certified for 256 ms refresh, and dies that fail the hot spec but pass cold are sold into this grade.
why: Fact 3 and yield: 4x less refresh and a new outlet for retention-weak dies that would otherwise be scrapped; rides on the liquid cooling already arriving with AI racks.

title: Phase-change thermal witness bits grade retired DRAM for second life
idea: Effect: thermal hysteresis (one-way amorphous-to-crystalline transitions). Each die holds a few chalcogenide witness cells of different compositions (Sb-rich, GeTe-rich, N-doped GST) that crystallize irreversibly after cumulative time above ~105/125/150 C, recording its thermal history. At datacenter decommission, a reader bins modules by witnessed stress plus a fast retention scan and resells them into edge, PC and CXL far-memory tiers at a derated refresh rate.
why: Usable supply: reclaims retired AI-server DDR/HBM on 3-5 year refresh cycles as trustworthy graded supply, maybe +10-20% effective bit supply with zero fab capex.

title: Compression-funded retention: saved bits buy stronger codes
idea: Ideal: ECC bits are free. Closest: each 64 B line is compressed (base-delta or frequent-pattern); lines that shrink by >=25% store a 4-error-correcting BCH code in the freed space and live in rows refreshed 8x less often, while incompressible lines stay in normal rows with SECDED.
why: Fact 3: on typical data (~60% compressible) refresh energy falls ~50% with no added parity storage.

title: RAID-5 inside the HBM stack ships dies with dead banks
idea: Combine storage RAID with die stacking: the base die stripes each cache line across N data dies plus rotating parity, so a stack with a dead bank or die region still works by reconstruction; known-bad regions are treated as erasures, which doubles correction power versus unknown errors.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): turning bad-bank stacks into sellable parts could recover much of that loss, cutting effective HBM cost/bit 10-25%.

title: Elastic twin-cell rows: weak rows fold into differential pairs
idea: Combine the 1T1C array with 2T2C twin-cell sensing, switchable per row: a mode bit in the row decoder makes rows containing weak cells store each bit as a complementary pair on adjacent bitlines, doubling signal and cancelling common-mode leakage at half capacity for those rows only; strong rows stay 1T1C.
why: Retention tail and charge wall (facts 1, 3): trades 50% capacity on the ~1-3% weak rows for ~2x sense margin instead of scrapping dies; allows lower Cs targets.

title: Eliminate fixed-function reliability: firmware-defined, fleet-learned refresh and ECC subscription
idea: Ship <=400 C BEOL memory modules whose refresh timing, reference levels, ECC codes and remap tables live in updatable controller firmware. The vendor learns drift models from fleet telemetry, pushes updates and sells this as a reliability subscription that raises usable capacity over time.
why: Lets vendors ship early, imperfectly characterized low-thermal-budget memories (as SSD makers do with NAND FTLs) while usable yield keeps improving; faster time-to-market for new memory.

title: Rope-maker's triplet: three distant weak cells fired as one bit
idea: A rope-maker twists three weak strands into a rope stronger than one thick strand: three small-capacitor cells at different physical positions on the same bitline are fired together (three wordlines driven at once) so their charges sum; a single leaky tail cell then removes only a third of the signal, and the sigma of the summed charge shrinks by sqrt(3).
why: Facts 1 and 3: each capacitor can drop to ~1.7 fF at far lower aspect ratio (easier etch), and tail-cell failures fall by orders of magnitude; density-neutral only if the smaller capacitors shrink the cell footprint.

title: Megasonic in-package anneal heals interface traps in cheap poly channels
idea: Effect: acoustically stimulated defect reconfiguration (ultrasound-induced interface-trap reduction in MOS structures). A transducer in the module periodically injects MHz acoustic energy into the 3D die, reordering and passivating traps in low-cost polysilicon thin-film access transistors and narrowing their leakage tail in the field (self-healing).
why: 10x density: poly-Si tiers cost far less per layer than single-crystal but have ~100x worse tails; healing them makes 40-tier poly-Si 3D DRAM (~10x) viable at the same cost.

title: Corrected-error patterns detect hammer instead of activation counting
idea: Reverse cause and effect: rather than counting activations, the controller spatially correlates corrected-error syndromes from scrubs and reads, using planted canary rows holding worst-case patterns; correctable flips clustering in rows R+1/R-1 identify R as an aggressor to throttle.
why: Row hammer: near-zero-area mitigation tuned to real chip vulnerability, suited to low-cost parts or as a backstop to counters.

title: Kintsugi conductor: liquid-metal microcapsules heal cracks in printed lines
idea: Kintsugi turns a crack into the strongest seam: microcapsules of gallium-indium liquid metal are blended into the printed silver interconnect ink of flexible memory foils and interposers, so when bending or thermal cycling cracks a line the capsules rupture and the liquid metal wicks into the gap, restoring conduction within milliseconds.
why: Line opens in printed and flexible circuits are a leading field failure; self-healing could cut them ~10x and allow cheaper, thinner foils.

title: CDN edge caching: weak memory tier holds only clean data
idea: Adapted from CDNs, which can lose a cached object because the origin always has a copy: the OS places only clean, file-backed pages (page cache, read-only model files, container images) on a pool of cheap low-grade DRAM with detection-only codes, and any detected error simply invalidates the page and refetches it from SSD.
why: Cost per bit (facts 3, 4): page cache is often 30-60% of server memory; serving it from salvaged or relaxed-spec DRAM frees premium DRAM for dirty data, and an error costs a ~50 us refetch instead of a crash.

title: MLC PCM resistance drift neutralized by co-written in-line reference cells
idea: Multi-level phase-change memory was abandoned largely because amorphous resistance drifts as t^0.1, collapsing level margins. Fix: each line writes three reference cells at the intermediate levels in the same pulse train, and reads compare data cells against those references, which drift identically, so thresholds track automatically.
why: Restores 2 bits/cell PCM (2x density) without periodic reprogramming.

title: Quantum-confined 2 nm channels widen bandgap and kill generation leakage
idea: Effect: quantum confinement. Access transistors of stacked lateral cells are ~2 nm-thick Si nanosheets in a Si/SiGe superlattice stack; confinement raises the effective bandgap ~0.3-0.4 eV, and because generation leakage scales ~exp(-Eg/2kT), off-state tails fall ~100-1000x, so ~0.5 fF suffices for 64 ms.
why: 10x density: no AR-75 capacitor and a 40-tier epitaxial superlattice stack (3D-NAND-style staircase) gives ~10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: one deep-etch module and epi replace the EUV-heavy capacitor and cell layers.

title: Mirror two glass arrays face-to-face; fastest CRC-clean copy wins
idea: Bond two glass memory panels face-to-face holding identical contents. Every read goes to both, and the first copy to pass its CRC is used, so a weak or busy cell on one side is simply ignored.
why: Reliability and tail latency: glass bits are cheap enough that 2x capacity for mirroring still undercuts silicon cost per bit; uncorrectable errors and tail latency drop together.

title: Rewritable repair maps in on-die MRAM replace laser fuses
idea: Rule: repairs must be redoable for the whole life of the part. One-time laser and e-fuse redundancy is replaced by a small on-die MRAM or FeFET repair table, so row and column remapping can be revised any number of times in the field and again at refurbishment, including undoing a repair onto a spare that later fails.
why: Turns redundancy from a one-shot fab resource into a lifelong repair budget, raising field survival and second-life yield.

title: Physarum tube-thickening: refresh flux follows observed error flow
idea: Slime mould thickens tubes that carry flow and lets idle ones wither; each subarray holds a refresh 'conductance' that increments whenever on-die ECC corrects an error there and decays geometrically otherwise, and the refresh scheduler splits its budget in proportion, so refresh converges onto where leakage actually lives.
why: Refresh overhead: most rows retain for seconds; concentrating the budget on the ~0.1% weak regions and tracking VRT/temperature drift automatically cuts refresh energy ~5-10x.

title: Plated-wire NDRO strip stores row-hammer counters without disturbing DRAM
idea: Plated-wire memory (UNIVAC 1110, Voyager) read non-destructively by tilting magnetization slightly and sensing its elastic return. Move DDR5 PRAC-style per-row activation counters out of the DRAM rows into a small magnetic or ferroelectric NDRO counter strip on the bank periphery, read without restore and updated in the background, so counting adds no read-modify-write timing and cannot itself be hammered.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): in-array PRAC counters cost ~10% of tRC and bandwidth; an NDRO strip keeps exact per-row counts without that penalty for ~1-2% area.

title: Nitrogen-deuterium hot isostatic press closes voids and passivates traps
idea: Castings are HIPed under argon to close porosity; instead, HIP finished DRAM wafers in 10-20 bar D2/N2 with no argon, so deuterium passivates interface traps (D-Si bonds resist hot-carrier and hammer-driven breaking better than H-Si) and the pressure collapses voids in capacitor fill.
why: Narrower leakage tail plus better hot-carrier and hammer robustness (facts 3, 9), rare-gas-free; target ~30% less refresh.

title: Wood-frog torpor: capacitorless vertical cells run cold to stretch retention
idea: Wood frogs survive freezing by slowing their chemistry; build capacitorless floating-body cells in a 3D-NAND-like vertical channel stack and run the memory in a sealed -40 C enclosure, where junction and GIDL leakage drop ~100-1000x so millisecond room-temperature retention becomes seconds.
why: Removes the capacitor (the costliest, highest-AR module) and borrows NAND-style stacking; trades cooling energy and enclosure cost for a target ~100x lower cost per GB at rack level.

title: Vinyl pre-emphasis: controller-boosted restore for flagged weak rows
idea: Adapted from vinyl recording's RIAA pre-emphasis, which boosts fragile high frequencies at cutting time so they survive playback: the controller keeps a small table of rows identified as weak and issues their writes and refreshes with extended tRAS/tWR (or back-to-back double activation) so their cells are fully restored to VARY instead of being truncated by tight default timings.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): many weak cells are under-restored rather than truly leaky; full restore on the ~0.1% flagged rows recovers ~10-20% charge and lets the whole device run a longer refresh interval, in controller firmware on existing chips.

title: Railway diverse redundancy: ECC parity stored in different physics
idea: SIL-4 railway signalling uses diverse channels so that no single cause can fail both. Keep data in the DRAM dies but store its ECC parity in SRAM or oxide-transistor gain cells on the HBM base die or logic die. Heat-driven retention collapse, a row-hammer burst or a die-level defect then cannot corrupt data and parity together.
why: Common-mode failures are what defeat ECC. With parity stored in a different technology, simpler codes cover correlated faults, permitting weaker DRAM cells and lighter hammer mitigation; the 12.5% of DRAM bits that held parity also become data (facts 1, 9).

title: Chef tastes and adjusts: in-line probing retunes ink chemistry mid-roll
idea: A chef tastes the sauce while it cooks: test structures printed every few meters of web are probed in-line (Vth, off-current, capacitance), and a feedback controller adjusts the next meters' oxide-precursor ink composition (e.g., Ga/Zn ratio), drop volume and flash-lamp energy, narrowing the device distribution in real time.
why: Variation, not mean performance, sets the ECC and redundancy overhead; halving sigma could halve spare and ECC overhead on printed memory and raise yield.

title: Musician tunes to the instrument: train models on each foil's error fingerprint
idea: A musician adapts to the quirks of one particular instrument: each printed memory foil's measured error statistics (which bits flip, in which direction, how often) feed a short fine-tuning pass of the neural network whose weights it will hold, so the model becomes robust to that foil's BER of 1e-3 to 1e-2 and needs no ECC.
why: The cheapest printed cells, with no ECC and minimal redundancy, can hold read-mostly AI weights; removes the 12.5% ECC overhead and most test cost, with an expected accuracy loss below 0.5%.

title: Maskless per-die repair wiring via domestic multi-beam e-beam
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics under the U.S.-only rule: after an early electrical test at first metal, a U.S.-built multi-column e-beam writer patterns a unique repair-routing layer per die that wires spare rows/columns in place of defective ones, with no fuses, lasers or masks.
why: Repair becomes layout instead of fuse banks (shrinking repair periphery, fact 7) and needs no foreign laser or scanner; yield rises because wiring defects fuses cannot fix become repairable.

title: Zone-refining sweep anneals one bank at a time on-die
idea: Zone refining drags a molten band through an ingot; after migrating a bank's data out, drive millisecond Joule pulses through its buried wordlines (or dedicated under-array heater lines) to locally anneal the bank, de-trapping the oxide and junction defects behind variable retention time, then sweep the hot zone to the next bank.
why: Resets VRT and leakage-tail degradation over life, so refresh can be set by the healthy distribution (~2x longer) and weak dies stay in service longer (fact 3).

title: Charge-sparse constant-weight encoding so most cells hold zero
idea: Reverse which state carries information: each 64 b word is encoded into an 80-cell constant-weight codeword with only ~25% charged cells, so ~75% of cells sit in the discharged state that cannot leak or be hammered; any 1->0 flip changes the weight, giving free detection.
why: Retention-vulnerable cells and hammer exposure drop ~2-3x and write energy falls; the ~25% capacity cost is repaid by permitting cheaper, weaker cells and longer refresh.

title: Substitute single write strength with weak working writes and power-fail consolidation
idea: Write ReRAM/MRAM cells weakly (low compliance current or short pulse) during operation for speed, low energy and high endurance, tracking 'weakly written' lines in a table; at power-fail or idle, a consolidation pass rewrites only those lines with strong retention pulses.
why: Endurance and energy: weak writes give ~10x endurance and ~3x lower energy, while only a small dirty fraction needs strong writes.

title: Charge-coupled circulating loops refresh by recirculation, no access transistors
idea: Effect: charge-coupled transfer. Bits are charge packets in short 64-stage CCD loops of gate-only electrodes over a buried channel (2F^2 per bit, no capacitor, no per-cell contact); packets circulate at ~2 GHz, and each lap passes a regenerator that restores packet size, so leakage and transfer inefficiency are corrected every ~30 ns. Many parallel loops give bandwidth, with ~16 ns average access.
why: 10x density: 2F^2 versus 6F^2 is 3x per layer, and 4 stacked thin-film CCD tiers give ~12x. Same cost: gates-only arrays need no capacitor module and no cell contacts.

title: Moving-target rows: keyed rolling remap defeats hammering
idea: Ideal: hammering is pointless because the aggressor never stays next to its victim. Closest: the DRAM keeps a secret keyed permutation of logical to physical rows and migrates one row per refresh slot to a new physical position, so any logical aggressor's physical neighbors change before ~1k activations can accumulate.
why: Fact 9: makes falling hammer thresholds irrelevant without per-row counters; costs one extra row copy per refresh slot (~1-2% bandwidth).

title: HZO nonvolatile shadow layer makes leaked cells recoverable
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite materials: a thin ferroelectric HfZrO sublayer (hafnium and zirconium from U.S. refiners) sits in series with the linear capacitor dielectric; before long idle periods data is copied into polarization and refresh stops, and on wake a polarization read restores the charge.
why: Refresh vanishes for idle regions (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) and retention-tail losses become recoverable; limited ferroelectric endurance is spent only on idle/wake transitions.

title: Speculative 0.3 V bitline read with ECC-triggered escalation
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: low-swing latch + slow offset-cancelled backup amp | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. The array runs at VARY 0.3 V with ~30 mV sense margin; on-die ECC checks every read and only failing codewords (~0.1%) are re-sensed by a slow, offset-cancelled high-gain amplifier and rewritten at 0.6 V.
why: Constraint/Fact 10: bitline CV^2 falls ~11x and escalations add <2%; reliability comes from detect-and-retry, not static margin.

title: Weak rows auto-morph into differential twin-cell pairs
idea: Worse: store a weak row's bits in single cells and hope. Flip: when a row's retention or margin drops below threshold, the DRAM pairs it with its neighbor row in a twin-cell (2T2C) mode where the two cells hold complementary charge on both bitline halves, doubling the sense signal at half capacity for just those rows.
why: Facts 1 and 3: converts the weak tail (~0.1-1% of rows) into reliable storage instead of spares or fuses, allowing smaller Cs at an affordable capacity cost.

title: Video error concealment for KV-cache and activation memory
idea: Adapted from video decoders that conceal lost macroblocks by interpolating from neighbors instead of stopping playback: KV-cache and activation buffers get one parity bit per 32-bit word, and when parity fails the runtime replaces the corrupted element with the mean of the same head's adjacent tokens (or zeroes it and renormalizes attention) instead of raising a machine check.
why: ECC overhead and refresh (facts 3, 8): detect-only parity costs ~3% instead of 12.5% and lets the cache run longer refresh at higher BER; transformers are robust to sparse token corruption, so the largest inference memory consumer moves to cheaper bits.

title: HARQ incremental redundancy: strong parity fetched only on decode failure
idea: LTE's HARQ sends extra redundancy only when the first decode fails. Light SEC-DED is stored inline, and strong BCH/RS incremental parity lives in a separate parity region in another bank. The controller fetches the strong parity only when the inline decode flags an uncorrectable error. Writes to the parity region are coalesced.
why: Strong correction (tolerating 10-100x more weak cells, so refresh can run 2-4x longer) at near-zero read-bandwidth cost (facts 3 and 5). FPGA demo on DDR5.

title: One-way street: Z-channel asymmetric codes for unidirectional hot retention errors
idea: At 125 C nearly all errors are charged-to-discharged; mapping every cell to logical polarity (true/anti cells) makes the channel a one-way Z-channel, and asymmetric codes correct t unidirectional errors with ~30-40% fewer parity bits than symmetric BCH.
why: Same ~6% overhead corrects ~2x more hot retention errors, allowing ~2x longer refresh at 125 C over the 10-year life.

title: Mars-rover autonomy: on-die repair agent remaps rows without the host
idea: Mars rovers repair faults on their own because Earth is 20 light-minutes away. Put a tiny state-machine agent and a 1-4K-entry CAM in the DRAM periphery or HBM base die. The agent watches on-die ECC syndromes, judges when a row or column is degrading, copies it to a spare during refresh slots and redirects its address. Repairs are reversible and continue for the whole life of the part, not just once at test.
why: In-field degradation (VRT, aging, hammer damage) turns into silent sparing. Dies with marginal rows can ship, giving ~2-5% yield and a several-fold cut in field DIMM replacements (facts 3, 9).

title: Pair-encoded ternary weights where every decay lands on zero
idea: Box [medium: capacitor pair per trit | access: planar | sense: dual-cell ternary sense | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Pruned AI weights are stored as +1 = cell A charged, -1 = cell B charged, 0 = both empty, so zero weights move no charge and every leakage event decays a weight toward 0 rather than flipping its sign.
why: Constraint: at 80-90% sparsity most cells move no charge on access or restore, ~5-10x lower energy; reliability: the only possible error direction is benign shrinkage.

title: Erasure-coded TSV lanes replace spare TSVs and repair fuses
idea: Combine network forward-error-correction with the TSV interface: data crosses the stack as Reed-Solomon codewords spread over all TSV lanes, so open or resistive TSVs are decoded as erasures in the base die instead of being steered to spare TSVs by fuses after test.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): removes spare-TSV area and repair-fuse test steps and tolerates in-field TSV failures; targets several points of stack yield and lower test cost.

title: Holographic spreading: Walsh-Hadamard encoding of tolerant data before storage
idea: Every fragment of a hologram holds a blurred copy of the whole image. The accelerator or controller applies a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform to each 64-value block before writing and clips on the inverse. A flipped bit then becomes small noise spread over 64 values instead of one catastrophic exponent error. It runs on existing hardware in firmware or kernels.
why: Error-tolerant data (activations, images) degrade gracefully in weak or rarely refreshed memory, giving refresh and ECC savings on 30-60% of AI capacity (fact 3).

title: Bubble-memory bootloop: self-stored subarray defect map replaces fuse banks
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with up to ~10% dead minor loops, listed in an on-chip 'bootloop' read at power-up. Design DRAM dies with ~12% spare subarrays and store the bad-subarray map in a few DRAM rows spread over several banks with 15x repetition coding, loaded into the address translator at boot and appended in the field as new failures appear.
why: Yield, periphery and capital (facts 4, 7): removes laser-fuse banks and lets aggressive cells or 3D tiers ship with clustered defects; ~15-25% more sellable dies per wafer at risky nodes.

title: Battery cell matching: retention-matched rank assembly
idea: Adapted from EV battery packs, which group cells of matched capacity so one weak cell does not limit the pack: dies are binned by measured retention (e.g., 64/128/256 ms classes) on existing testers, modules are assembled only from same-class dies, and the class is written to SPD so the controller sets tREFI per rank instead of for the worst die in a mixed rank.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): today one weak die forces worst-case refresh on its whole rank; matched ranks let 60-80% of modules run 2-4x longer refresh, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss with only assembly-flow changes.

title: Write-timestamp decay model slides gain-cell read thresholds
idea: Storage-gate voltage in a gain cell decays along a self-limiting, near-logarithmic subthreshold curve, V(t) ~ V0 - S*log10(1+t/tau). Store a 6-bit write epoch per row and place the read reference at the model's predicted midpoint for that age. The deterministic decay is then removed, and only the stochastic spread uses margin.
why: Capacitorless retention: refresh intervals 5-10x longer, so weak gain cells become acceptable.

title: Negative-capacitance ferroelectric gate steepens access-transistor turn-off
idea: Effect: ferroelectric negative capacitance. A thin Zr-doped HfO2 layer in the buried-wordline gate stack, capacitance-matched to the gate oxide, gives sub-60 mV/dec swing over the off region, so for the same on-current the tail off-leakage falls ~10x (or the wordline overdrive falls from ~3 V toward 2 V).
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) plus voltage floor (fact 10): ~4x+ retention, or ~30% lower wordline CV^2 energy.

title: Old radio repairman: self-clearing printed electrodes isolate capacitor shorts
idea: Old metallized-film capacitors heal themselves: storage-capacitor top electrodes are printed as ultrathin (~20 nm) metal films, and a one-time clearing pulse at test vaporizes the electrode around any pinhole short in the printed dielectric, isolating it with negligible capacitance loss instead of killing the cell or the whole line.
why: Dielectric pinholes are the main shorting defect in printed high-k capacitors; self-clearing turns hard shorts into ~1% capacitance loss and allows thinner, higher-capacitance printed dielectrics.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM vault where cells never forget
idea: Ideal: memory that never forgets. Closest: run 180 nm-era DRAM dies immersed at 77 K, where subthreshold and junction leakage fall by many orders so retention reaches hours, refresh disappears and the tail vanishes; the vault serves as a large refresh-free capacity tier.
why: Fact 3 and supply: refresh-free and tail-free on legacy fabs; cryocooling cost is partly offset by the removed refresh and relaxed cell design.

title: DUV quad-patterning with a doubled overlay budget in mature fabs
idea: Po: make leading-edge memory in a trailing-edge fab. U.S. 28-40 nm-class fabs with immersion DUV run SAQP for the cell layers with overlay tolerances relaxed 2x; the resulting systematic misaligned contacts (~0.5-1% of cells) are mapped and corrected as erasures.
why: U.S. manufacturability and EUV independence (fact 4): ~16-18 nm-class cell density from existing U.S. tooling at roughly a third of an EUV DRAM fab's capex.

title: Refurb-phone economy: second-life server DIMMs behind CXL with host codes
idea: Refurbishers in emerging markets turn worn parts into working phones. Harvest DDR4/DDR5 RDIMMs from decommissioned servers, re-screen them, and mount them in CXL Type-3 expanders whose controller adds stronger chipkill-plus codes and patrol scrub. Hyperscalers get a cold memory tier at a fraction of new-DIMM cost.
why: Adds supply without wafers. Millions of DIMMs are shredded every year, and reuse with stronger codes for aged cells could cover 5-15% of cold-tier demand (capital and scarce-resource intensity).

title: Hot-swap CXL memory bricks with erasure-coded striping
idea: Rule: any memory unit must be removable for repair while the system runs. Pages are striped with RS(8+2) across 10 CXL memory bricks, so any brick can be pulled live, repaired or replaced, and rebuilt in the background onto a hot spare.
why: Tolerates whole-device failure at 20% overhead. Lets cheap, unqualified or second-life DRAM serve production pools, raising usable supply.
